evidence_notes.finding: A PRISMA review of 121 studies concludes that the binding constraints on LLM multi-agent systems are architectural rather than model-level: evaluation standardization, long-horizon reliability, communication security, interoperability, cost-efficient orchestration, governance, and system-level interpretability. It argues agent systems must be evaluated as holistic architectures rather than by benchmarking the base LLM in isolation.
evidence_notes.quote:
The literature review suggests that these challenges are beyond 
the capabilities of individual language models and include evaluation standardization, long -horizon reliability, 
security, interoperability, communication efficiency, governance, and interpretability.

extraction.framework: LangChain/LangGraph, AutoGPT, AutoGen, MetaGPT, CAMEL, ChatDev, CrewAI (surveyed); MCP, A2A, ANP interoperability protocols
extraction.benchmark: REALM-Bench discussed as an example of long-horizon multi-agent evaluation; no benchmark run by the authors
extraction.key_results: PRISMA screening of 1,034 records (Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, IEEE Xplore, Jan 2020-Mar 2026) yielded 121 included studies. Contributes a framework taxonomy tracing modular chain-based execution to stateful graph-based and autonomous orchestration, a taxonomy of hierarchical, peer-to-peer, and role-based collaboration architectures, and an explicit separation of internal message-level, shared-state, and graph-based coordination from cross-system interoperability protocols (MCP for agent-to-tool, A2A for agent-to-agent, ANP for decentralized discovery, with ACP converged into A2A). Identifies error accumulation over long trajectories and cross-agent contamination as distinct multi-agent risks, and calls for intermediate verification checkpoints, confidence-aware routing, rollback, redundant agent validation, adaptive replanning, and explicit termination policies.
extraction.limitations: Narrative thematic synthesis with only qualitative methodological appraisal; no meta-analysis, effect sizes, or quantitative comparison across frameworks. The authors note that primary studies use incompatible tasks, metrics, model configurations, tool environments, and stopping conditions, which prevents direct comparison. Supplementary authoritative sources published after the March 2026 cutoff and pre-2020 foundational works were consulted but excluded from PRISMA counts. Non-English, non-peer-reviewed, and classical non-LLM multi-agent work was excluded.

evidence_notes.finding: The survey identifies an evaluation vacuum: no widely adopted benchmark targets multi-agent orchestration itself, so coordination quality, communication efficiency, delegation appropriateness, and cost are unmeasured while only task outcomes are scored. It names task duplication, contradictory outputs, and convergence failure as the three canonical coordination failure modes whose frequency rises with agent count.
evidence_notes.quote: The field evaluates what agents produce, not how well they collaborate.

extraction.framework: LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen/Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK, MetaGPT, DSPy, AgentScope, GPTSwarm, DyLAN; MCP, A2A, ANP protocols
extraction.benchmark: SWE-bench and SWE-bench Verified, GAIA, WebArena, OSWorld, HumanEval, AgentBench, tau-bench (reviewed, not re-run)
extraction.baseline: human baselines on each benchmark; single-agent LLM systems as reference
extraction.key_results: Proposes a three-topology (centralized, decentralized, hierarchical) plus one adaptivity-axis taxonomy and a six-dimension coordination-quality evaluation framework. Reports large agent-human gaps: GAIA 15% for GPT-4 with plugins versus 92% human, WebArena 14.41% versus 78.24%, OSWorld 12.24% versus 72.36%, and tau-bench pass^8 reliability below 25% in retail. MetaGPT's publish-subscribe SOP design reaches 85.9% HumanEval at 124.3 tokens per line versus ChatDev's 248.9. DyLAN reports a 25.0% MMLU gain from pruning weak agents rather than adding capacity, inverting the assumption that more agents is better. Trajectory reduction cuts input tokens 40-60% within 1-2% of baseline performance. Prompt Infection shows malicious prompts self-replicating across interconnected agents, and 25 of 30 surveyed deployed agentic systems disclose no internal safety evaluation.
extraction.limitations: Explicitly a structured narrative survey rather than a systematic review, with no registered protocol, dual-reviewer screening, or GRADE evidence grading. Several headline adoption and market figures are flagged by the authors as vendor-reported or analyst projections. Most cited benchmark results used GPT-4 or GPT-4o backbones, so both absolute numbers and the relative ranking of orchestration approaches may not transfer. The authors note that self-reported efficiency claims from MetaGPT and GPTSwarm are unverified by any independent benchmark and that cross-system comparisons are rarely apples-to-apples. Literature cutoff March 2026.

evidence_notes.finding: The survey states the multi-agent advantage is conditional on collaboration design rather than intrinsic: well-designed collaboration channels let multi-agent systems beat single agents, but a poorly designed competitive multi-agent system can be beaten by a single agent given strong prompts.
evidence_notes.quote:
On the other hand, as studied in [ 128] MAS approach with suboptimal design for their
competitive collaboration channels can be overtaken by single-agent counterpart with
strong prompts.

extraction.framework: AutoGen, CAMEL, CrewAI, MapCoder, MACRec, Solo Performance Prompting, Auto-GPT (surveyed)
extraction.baseline: single-agent methods including chain-of-thought prompting and strongly prompted single agents
extraction.key_results: Introduces an extensible framework characterising collaboration channels by actors, type (cooperation, competition, coopetition), structure (peer-to-peer, centralized, distributed), strategy (role-based, rule-based, model-based), and coordination protocol, plus static versus dynamic orchestration architectures. Reports that sequentially chained specialist plus summarizer agents outperform single-agent chain-of-thought on college-level science questions, while noting the converse case where a suboptimally designed competitive MAS loses to a strongly prompted single agent. Distils six lessons: effective collaboration channels, collective domain knowledge, adaptive role and channel assignment, matching rule-based/role-based/model-based strategies to task type, scalability, and ethics/safety. Surveys applications across 5G/6G and Industry 5.0, question answering, and social and cultural domains.
extraction.limitations: The authors note LLMs are standalone algorithms not trained for collaboration, leaving the mechanisms by which collaboration helps unclear and agent behaviour hard to explain or predict for stakeholders. They flag safety and performance failures such as exploitation and hallucination in competitive scenarios, and rising coordination complexity, cost, and performance degradation as agent count grows. No quantitative pooling, no standardized benchmark, and no controlled single-versus-multi experiment is performed by the survey itself.

evidence_notes.finding: A MetaGPT-versus-ChatDev case study shows that replacing dialogue-driven coordination with a hierarchical SOP pipeline using structured document handoffs cuts end-to-end latency by roughly 29% and simultaneously improves output executability, so coordination topology is a first-order determinant of both speed and reliability.
evidence_notes.quote:
The data in Table 11 reveals that MetaGPT completes
complex software development tasks in significantly less
time (541 s vs. 762 s on average), representing a ∼ 29%
reduction in end-to-end latency [26].

extraction.framework: MetaGPT (hierarchical SOP case study), ChatDev (chat-based baseline), DyLAN, AgentScope, TimeArena
extraction.agent_count: 5 role agents in the MetaGPT case study (Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager, Engineer, QA Engineer)
extraction.benchmark: SoftwareDev benchmark (7 representative tasks, numbers sourced from the MetaGPT paper); TimeArena cited as a simulation environment
extraction.baseline: ChatDev chat-based multi-agent coordination; single-agent architectures discussed as the contrasting paradigm
extraction.key_results: Decomposes end-to-end latency into core inference, agent framework, system/infrastructure, and multi-agent coordination layers, and names five multi-agent latency sources: inter-agent communication round trips, synchronization overhead, coordination protocol delays, cascading delays in dependent tasks, and straggler heterogeneity. Case study: MetaGPT 541 s versus ChatDev 762 s (~29% lower), executability 3.75 versus 2.25 on a 1-4 scale, and human revision cost 0.83 versus 2.5 manual corrections, which the authors treat as reduced hidden latency. Reports hierarchical decomposition at 10-30 s subtask granularity achieving 50-70% critical-path latency reduction over flat structures, dynamic load balancing yielding 20-40% throughput gains, and trajectory reduction cutting input tokens 40-60% within 1-2% of original performance. Notes the rigid SOP workflow trades adaptability for speed and suits only domains with well-defined roles.
extraction.limitations: The authors state that standardized MAS latency benchmarks comparable to single-agent TTFT/TPOT do not yet exist, and that fine-grained communication and coordination overheads are not measured consistently across architectures. They explicitly note that multi-agent coordination mechanisms are rarely evaluated against single-agent baselines under controlled conditions, so the relative contribution of each optimization layer is obscured. Case-study numbers are secondary, drawn from the MetaGPT paper over only seven SoftwareDev tasks rather than independently replicated. Aggressive latency optimizations risk degrading accuracy, factual consistency, and safety, a latency-quality-safety trade-off the survey leaves unquantified, and system-level optimizations are often hardware-specific and non-portable.

evidence_notes.finding: A seven-agent, on-premises AutoGen pipeline applied to 2.12M lines of COBOL, MUMPS, and PeopleSoft legacy code across three universities achieved 87% behavioural equivalence with 35% manual intervention, versus a cited single-LLM GPT-4 COBOL study where 72% of function-level translations succeeded but only 34% achieved end-to-end behavioural equivalence.
evidence_notes.quote:
An average behavioural equivalence of 87% was achieved, with the highest accuracy (91%) 
observed in the large research university deployment, confirming strong functional preservation across diverse systems 
[Table 9].

extraction.framework: AutoGen (primary, scored 8.5/10), LangGraph (secondary); custom seven-agent on-premises modernization architecture with local Llama 3/Mixtral inference
extraction.benchmark: Proprietary multi-institutional legacy corpus: 2.3M lines reduced to 1.8M analyzable lines across COBOL mainframe SIS, MUMPS registration, PeopleSoft customizations, and PL/I; 47 regulatory requirements and 3,421 test cases
extraction.baseline: Traditional manual/consultant-led modernization (65-75% manual intervention, 40-50% documentation accuracy); a cited 2024 single-LLM GPT-4 COBOL study as the monolithic comparator
extraction.key_results: 2.12M lines analyzed produced 2.04M lines of modernized Java, Python, and Go with 87% aggregate behavioural equivalence (91% / 84% / 86% by site). Manual intervention fell to 35% versus 65-75% traditional, timelines fell 65% (3,600 hours at 30 FTE to 552 hours, an 85% activity-level reduction), documentation accuracy reached 78% versus 40-50%, and 12-month cost fell from $1,105,000 to $468,000 (58%). Agent task success ranged 87.2% (code generation, 2.7 average retries) to 96.9% (compliance validation, 1.0 retries). Compliance validation reached 93.6% FERPA, 97.9% GDPR, 100% CCPA, and 95.7% institutional policy. Processing scaled near-linearly from 6.2 days at 500K lines to 17.5 days at 2.1M lines. The paper's distinctive claim is governance alignment: mapping agent tiers onto academic committees, senate subcommittees, and IT steering committees to reduce adoption resistance.
extraction.limitations: Pilot spans only three institutional partners, and the authors themselves call for 20-30 institutions before statistical generalization. No matched single-agent or single-LLM arm was run by the authors; the 65-75% manual-intervention and 40-50% documentation comparators are traditional-practice figures and the 34% end-to-end equivalence figure is drawn from a cited third-party study, so the headline contrast is not a controlled comparison. Code generation showed the highest failure and retry rates. Llama 3 context-window limits required hierarchical summarization as a workaround. All outcome metrics are self-reported from the authors' own deployment without independent verification, blinding, or variance estimates.

evidence_notes.finding: A four-agent LangGraph RAG pipeline for entity resolution beat a single-LLM GPT-4 baseline on accuracy (93.9% vs 86.9%) while simultaneously cutting tokens ~62%, API calls >60%, and runtime 52%, attributed to selective retrieval per agent and shared state memory that avoids redundant inference.
evidence_notes.quote:
The proposed framework reduced token
usage by approximately 62% and API calls by over 60% compared to the single-LLM baseline, leading
to a 52% decrease in average runtime.

extraction.framework: LangGraph-orchestrated multi-agent RAG (Direct Matcher, Indirect Matcher, Household Matcher, Move Detector) over FAISS/Qdrant with GPT-4o-mini, Mistral, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Llama 3.2, and DeepSeek
extraction.benchmark: Synthetic S12PX administrative/census dataset segments of 200-300 records with duplicates and injected data-quality faults; precision, recall, F1, pairwise P/R, Adjusted Rand Index, runtime, and expert-rated interpretability
extraction.baseline: Single-LLM entity resolution (GPT-4); rule-based deterministic matching; FAISS-only vector similarity; hybrid no-RAG ablation; uncoordinated multi-LLM
extraction.key_results: 93.9% accuracy, 94.6% precision, 92.3% recall, 93.4% F1, versus single-LLM GPT-4 at 86.9/88.4/84.5/86.4, hybrid no-RAG at 89.2, FAISS-only at 84.6, and rule-based at 78.5. Per-agent accuracy ranged 91.3% (Move Detector) to 94.3% (Direct Matcher). Efficiency: 14,506 tokens versus 38,400, 112 API calls versus 287, and 94.5 s versus 198.4 s per 300 records. The uncoordinated multi-LLM ablation reached only 23% cost reduction versus 61% for the coordinated framework, isolating orchestration rather than agent count as the driver. Residual errors were dominated by data quality (ambiguous name variants 27%, incomplete temporal information 18%, address formatting 16%) with LLM misinterpretation and context drift accounting for only 9%, which the authors attribute to retrieval grounding suppressing hallucination.
extraction.limitations: Scalability was tested only on subsets of roughly 300 entities because of LLM context and API constraints, so production-scale behaviour on millions of records is unvalidated. Evaluation used synthetic S12PX data rather than live administrative or census records, leaving cross-source generalization untested. Agent reasoning remains sensitive to prompt wording and context-window size, prompting the authors to call for adaptive prompt optimization. Sequential inter-agent orchestration introduces latency that the authors propose to mitigate with future parallel execution. Quantitative metrics were averaged over only three runs. The retrieved full text is the Preprints.org version marked not peer reviewed.

evidence_notes.finding: A five-dimension taxonomy derived from 18 systematic studies and 14 frameworks finds that architectural primitives (agents, tools, memory, roles) are mature while monitoring, KPI/value-addition modelling, human feedback, continual evolution, benchmarking, and agent discovery are largely unimplemented, making the robustness of agentic software-engineering solutions hard to justify or reproduce.
evidence_notes.quote:
Governance mechanisms introduce a trade-off between
flexibility and controllability.

extraction.framework: 14 analyzed LMAS frameworks (workflow-oriented, graph-based, and tool-augmented, including LangChain/LangGraph and LlamaIndex); README summarization exemplar built on LangChain
extraction.agent_count: 4 in the README summarization exemplar (Extractor, Summarizer, Teacher, Prompt Creator)
extraction.benchmark: ROUGE-scored GitHub README 'About' summarization against curated ground-truth descriptions
extraction.baseline: Single-model README summarization, described qualitatively as struggling with heterogeneous structure and extreme length variability
extraction.key_results: Taxonomy organizes the design space into Core Architecture, Governance Rules, Agent Monitoring, Behavioral Models, and Reusability, refined from 57 initial concepts to 21 sub-concepts. Coverage analysis shows Agent, Objective, Action, and Role are supported by essentially all 18 papers and 14 frameworks, whereas Value-addition/KPI modelling appears in only 4 frameworks, Continual evolution in 1, Benchmarking in 5, Agent comparison in 6, and Discovery in 3. All surveyed frameworks support only text-based agent-environment interfaces. The exemplar pairs GPT-4o-mini for high-volume extraction and summarization with GPT-4o for reasoning-intensive teacher and prompt-creator roles, using ROUGE gates for reproducibility. The paper argues MAS should be treated as engineered software systems with explicit, comparable design decisions.
extraction.limitations: Corpus is small and narrow: 47 initial records reduced to 18 primary studies plus 14 frameworks, restricted to English systematic studies in well-ranked venues or relevant preprints from January 2023 to January 2025, searched only in Scopus, and excluding workshops, posters, non-systematic studies, and non-LLM MAS. The taxonomy is conceptual and validated only against a single illustrative README summarization case, with no controlled evaluation or inter-rater reliability reported. The authors explicitly defer security, cost management, and ethics dimensions to future work due to space limits.

evidence_notes.finding: A three-agent retriever/reasoner/summarizer pipeline outscored a monolithic single-agent Gemini setup on every reference-overlap metric, but the single-agent arm answered without access to the supporting explanation documents that the multi-agent retriever consumed, so the reported gap confounds retrieval augmentation with multi-agent decomposition.
evidence_notes.quote:
As shown in the Table 1 the Multi agent system 
outperform the single agent system in every metrics.

extraction.framework: Custom single-agent versus three-agent RAG pipeline (Retriever Agent, Reasoner Agent, Summarizer Agent) on Google gemini-flash-latest
extraction.benchmark: Author-created CSV dataset of three basic science topics (photosynthesis, water cycle, respiration) with query, reference answer, and supporting explanation per row; scored with BLEU, ROUGE-1/2/L, METEOR, and BERTScore
extraction.baseline: single-agent monolithic LLM answering each query directly with no intermediate reasoning
extraction.key_results: Multi-agent beat single-agent on all six metrics: BERTScore F1 0.8978 versus 0.8117, BLEU 0.1124 versus 0.0036, METEOR 0.5867 versus 0.1749, ROUGE-1 0.5489 versus 0.0829, ROUGE-2 0.2966 versus 0.0211, ROUGE-L 0.4636 versus 0.0675. The authors conclude that LLM framework performance depends on structure and task assignment rather than model size alone, and that decomposing goals into modular subtasks reduces hallucination in complex multi-requirement tasks.
extraction.limitations: The paper reports no limitations section. Observed threats: the dataset is tiny, hand-authored, and covers only three elementary science topics; the paper states the single-agent system responded without accessing the supporting documents while the multi-agent setup retrieved, reasoned, and summarized over them, so retrieval access is confounded with architecture; no repeated runs, variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported; no token, cost, or latency measurement despite the paper's 'efficiency' framing; a single model family is used; and the reduced-hallucination claim is asserted rather than measured. The extracted text also contains a garbled encoded column alongside a readable one.

evidence_notes.finding: Because the split-knowledge tasks are constructed so no single agent can solve them, the study deliberately omits any single-agent baseline and instead isolates routing: belief-guided Thompson-sampling delegation matched random delegation on success (96.65% vs 96.46%) while using 0.72x tokens, 0.83x agent calls, and 0.81x time-to-success.
evidence_notes.quote:
Since split-knowledge tasks are unsolvable by any single
agent, single-agent baselines are excluded by task design.

extraction.framework: REDEREF: training-free controller with Thompson-sampling belief-guided delegation, calibrated LLM/programmatic judge, evidence-based selection, and memory-aware priors
extraction.agent_count: 16 (6 specialist RAG agents plus 10 generalist conversational agents)
extraction.benchmark: Author-constructed split-knowledge benchmark synthesized in three stages so each task requires non-redundant contributions from 4-6 agents; Azure OpenAI endpoints with fixed seeds
extraction.baseline: Random (uniform) delegation inside an otherwise identical recursive loop; single-agent baselines explicitly excluded by task design
extraction.key_results: At matched success (96.65% versus 96.46%) REDEREF used 0.72x tokens, 0.83x agent calls, and 0.81x time-to-first-success relative to random delegation. Removing belief updates raised use of underperforming agents by 17.2% and exploratory attempts by 8.2%, both significant under paired bootstrap at p<0.01. Specialization emerged: median belief for the electrical-engineering expert rose from 0.50 to 0.84 over 55 tasks while rounds-to-expert-selection fell from 8.11 to 6.86. Under enforced impairment the Biology agent's belief fell from 0.35 to 0.23 and its contributions dropped from 12 to 0, with system output quality degrading only from 84.52 to 81.80, demonstrating graceful rather than catastrophic degradation. Quality gains peaked with 3-5 contributing agents, not with more. A regret bound of O(sqrt(N T log T)/delta) quantifies how judge noise inflates routing regret by exactly 1/delta.
extraction.limitations: The authors state REDEREF depends critically on judge reliability, and that documented biases in machine adjudication can distort competency updates and entrench suboptimal routing. Sequential recursion adds latency, limiting real-time applicability. Cold-start behaviour resembles random delegation until evidence accumulates. Because recursive retry already saturates success on the suite, task success is treated as a constraint rather than an outcome, so the study measures efficiency and not capability. Adaptive down-weighting may prematurely exclude competent agents during temporary performance fluctuations. Evaluation is on synthetic split-knowledge tasks rather than real software engineering workloads, and no single-agent comparison is possible by construction.

evidence_notes.finding: Across 900 Monte Carlo runs, splitting scoring from explanation into two agents preserved reliability (ICC(1,k) = 0.9921) and sharply raised grounding and coherence, but introduced a small statistically significant contradiction rate (0.031, d = 0.43) between the scoring and explanation agents, evidencing a measurable coordination cost of decomposition.
evidence_notes.quote:
Empirical evidence from 900 Monte Carlo executions conﬁrms that multi -agent
architectural decomposition preserves psychometric robustness ( ICC ≈ 0.99) while
substantially enhancing semantic grounding and coherence.

extraction.framework: TRACE-ED transparency framework applied to a single-agent grader versus a two-agent grader that separates scoring from explanation
extraction.benchmark: Monte Carlo design over 10 synthetic short-answer responses x 3 rubric indicators x multiple temperature settings x 15 repetitions = 900 runs; ICC(1,k), Grounding Rate, Coherence Score, Contradiction Rate, Jaccard structural stability, Welch's t-tests and Cohen's d
extraction.baseline: single-agent LLM producing score and explanation in one call
extraction.key_results: Multi-agent ICC(1,k) = 0.9921, above the 0.90 high-stakes threshold, while the single-agent arm showed zero within-answer variance. Grounding Rate rose from 0.000 to 0.763 (t = -55.76, p = 6.03e-204, d = 3.72) and Coherence Score from 0.000 to 0.782 (t = -118.52, p < 0.001, d = 7.90). Contradiction Rate rose from 0.000 to 0.031 (t = -6.47, p = 2.61e-10, d = 0.43). The authors conclude transparency is an architecture-sensitive vector that modular decomposition redistributes rather than uniformly maximizes, and that interpretability and reliability are not inherently in tension.
extraction.limitations: Uses only 10 synthetic short-answer responses in a single domain with one LLM family, and the authors call for validation on real classroom datasets, diverse subjects, and multiple LLM families. The single-agent arm scored exactly 0.000 on both grounding and coherence and had zero within-answer variance, which suggests those metrics may be degenerate for the single-agent operationalization rather than reflecting a graded architectural difference, inflating the reported effect sizes. Code and data are available only on request. No cost, latency, or token accounting is reported. Preprint on Research Square, not peer reviewed.

evidence_notes.finding: A conceptual role-based architecture pairs redundant small language models per SWEBOK requirements-analysis subtask under a supervisory LLM arbitrator, and its probabilistic model shows that with four independent subprocesses at per-step reliability 0.5 the overall success probability collapses to 0.0625, so acceptable end-to-end reliability requires per-step reliability above 0.90.
evidence_notes.quote:
However, introducing 
multiple agents also raises challenges related to coordination, 
validation, and decision reliability.

extraction.framework: Proposed conceptual role-based LLM-supervisor / paired-SLM architecture with redundancy-based double checking and uncertainty-aware arbitration
extraction.agent_count: 2 paired SLM agents per task under 1 supervisory LLM, across 4 SWEBOK subprocesses
extraction.key_results: Decomposes SWEBOK requirements analysis into four analytical roles (basic requirements analysis, quality-of-service economics, formal analysis, conflict resolution) executed in parallel by paired SLMs. Acceptance uses a two-level check: report-level comparison against a similarity threshold epsilon, then supervisory arbitration favouring whichever of LLM or SLM has lower uncertainty sigma. Under independence, total success is the product of per-step probabilities, so P = 0.5 per step across four steps yields 0.0625 overall, demonstrating rapid reliability decay and implying a P > 0.90 per-step requirement. The paper frames redundancy plus hierarchical supervision as a mechanism to limit ambiguity and error propagation in the earliest, most error-prone SDLC phase.
extraction.limitations: The authors state the contribution is predominantly theoretical and exploratory, with no implemented framework, dataset, or empirical evaluation and no claim of empirical validation. The probabilistic argument assumes statistical independence between SLM correctness and between subprocesses, which the authors acknowledge does not strictly hold. No operational definition or measurement procedure is given for the uncertainty metric sigma or the similarity threshold epsilon, and the negative case D- is explicitly not considered. No single-agent comparison is performed.

evidence_notes.finding: In an industrial CloudOps deployment, replacing a monolithic single-LLM RAG system with the six-agent MOYA framework improved every automated metric against SME gold-standard answers and cut human-reported defects from 22 to 15, with the largest gain in misclassification; despite consuming more tokens, the multi-agent system was faster end-to-end.
evidence_notes.quote:
MOY A Framework outperformed the monolithic baseline
in key areas, especially in metrics focused on semantic align-
ment (e.g., METEOR and BERTScore), indicating enhanced
interpretative capabilities.

extraction.framework: MOYA (Meta Orchestrator Of Your Agents): Core Engine with Request Handler, Orchestrator, Agent Selector, Agent Registry, Lifecycle Manager, Context Memory, and guardrails
extraction.agent_count: 6 (Static, Summary, Report, plus Notification, Cost, and Dashboard API agents), each deployed as a serverless function
extraction.benchmark: 260 CloudOps prompts (26 SME-curated seeds x 10 LLM-generated paraphrases) scored with ROUGE-1, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore against SME gold-standard responses, plus an 8-person practitioner bug-identification session
extraction.baseline: Monolithic single-LLM RAG system (the team's own prior production implementation)
extraction.key_results: MOYA beat the monolith on every automated metric: ROUGE-1 0.448 versus 0.321, BLEU 0.221 versus 0.102, METEOR 0.423 versus 0.265, and BERTScore F1 0.868 versus 0.843, with the largest gains on the semantic metrics. Human evaluation with four product managers and four platform engineers found 15 issues in MOYA versus 22 in the monolith, with a marked reduction in misclassification attributed to targeted agent routing, though formatting issues became the dominant residual category and were later mitigated by refining per-agent system prompts. Contrary to the authors' expectation, the multi-agent system achieved faster response times despite higher input and output token consumption, an accepted efficiency trade-off. A hierarchical summary-of-summaries strategy with multi-threaded parallel LLM calls addressed context-length limits on large cloud workloads.
extraction.limitations: The authors report internal validity risk from agent-invocation accuracy, noting that classification precision may degrade as the number of agents grows. External validity is limited to AWS-based environments, with transfer to Azure, GCP, or hybrid estates uncertain because of API, workflow, and data-format variation. Construct validity is threatened by rapid LLM version churn producing inconsistent behaviour across releases, and by LLM hallucination of counts and configurations such as cloud instance numbers, which existing cross-check mechanisms may not fully catch. Evaluation rests on a single 260-prompt curated dataset and an internal, non-blinded bug session by the vendor's own staff.

evidence_notes.finding: A four-specialist debate framework with Moderator and Judge lifted accuracy from 67.00% (single-agent direct prompting) and 90.70% (single-agent chain-of-thought) to 93.90%, largely by eliminating indecisive 'uncertain' outputs, but average inference time rose from 4.7 s to 37.5 s, roughly an eightfold latency cost.
evidence_notes.quote:
PhishDebate outperforms both baselines across
all key evaluation metrics, achieving the highest precision
(90.57%), accuracy (93.90%), recall (98.00%), and F1
score (94.14%).

extraction.framework: PhishDebate (URL Analyst, HTML Structure, Content Semantic, and Brand Impersonation agents coordinated by a Moderator with a final Judge, configurable 1-10 debate rounds and early termination)
extraction.benchmark: Mendeley Phishing Websites dataset and TR-OP dataset, 500 phishing plus 500 legitimate samples each; TPR, TNR, FPR, FNR, precision, recall, accuracy, F1, and inference time
extraction.baseline: Single-agent direct prompting and single-agent chain-of-thought prompting, both on GPT-4o-mini
extraction.key_results: On GPT-4o-mini, PhishDebate reached precision 90.57%, accuracy 93.90%, recall 98.00%, F1 94.14%, versus single agent 60.57/67.00/97.40/74.69 and CoT 88.61/90.70/93.40/90.94. CoT produced 50 'uncertain' outputs (16 phishing, 34 legitimate) counted as misclassifications, a reliability failure the debate mechanism removed. Latency rose from 4.7 s (single agent) to 10.5 s (CoT) to 37.5 s (PhishDebate), though 1,000 samples cost only about $3.357. Ablation showed the ensemble is not monotonically beneficial: removing the HTML Structure Agent raised F1 to 0.9471 and accuracy to 0.9455 while the full configuration retained the best recall (0.985), and removing the URL Analyst dropped recall to 0.952. Across models GPT-4o was most balanced (96.50% accuracy), while Gemini-2.0 violated the binary-output instruction on 8 legitimate sites, pushing its false-positive rate to 14.4% - an instruction-following failure rather than a detection failure. A two-round case study shows two agents reversing their stance to reach consensus.
extraction.limitations: The authors note that debate-agent performance ultimately reflects the biases and knowledge gaps of the underlying LLMs, bounded by pre-training data. Commercial API input-length restrictions force HTML and visible-text truncation, causing potential information loss. All experiments used commercial APIs, so the claimed feasibility of local deployment for cost and latency reduction is untested. Adversarial robustness against obfuscation, cloaking, and adversarially crafted pages is deferred to future work. The 8x latency increase over the single-agent baseline is reported but not framed as a limitation.

evidence_notes.finding: The report argues multi-agent deployment transforms rather than merely adds to the risk landscape, naming six failure modes (cascading reliability failures, inter-agent communication failures, monoculture collapse, conformity bias, deficient theory of mind, mixed-motive dynamics), and prescribes explicit single-agent baselining to test whether coordination actually improves performance at all.
evidence_notes.quote:
Compare multi-agent outcomes against individual agents
working on decomposable portions of the task to determine if coordination actually
improves performance.

extraction.baseline: Recommends four reference baselines: single-agent performance on decomposable task portions, human team benchmarks, theoretical optima, and historical performance at initial deployment
extraction.key_results: Defines four canonical settings (single-agent equivalent, centralized orchestrator with specialised delegates, collaborative swarm, distributed autonomous task force) and maps six failure modes onto them. Argues that a collection of safe agents does not guarantee a safe collection of agents, and that every multi-agent system inherits single-agent failure modes plus additional cascading and emergent layers, making single-agent analysis an essential baseline. Centres risk analysis on validity - construct, external, content, and consequential - pursued through progressively increasing convergent evidence across simulations, observational data analysis, benchmarking against baselines, red teaming, and capability benchmarking, with staged testing that gradually increases exposure. Notes that in a centralized orchestrator the orchestrator's cognitive limits become system-wide bottlenecks because delegates lack visibility of the full task. Red-teaming recipes include malformed instructions, contradictory goals, information asymmetries, and inserting a malfunctioning or adversarial agent to test cascade resilience. Also flags LLM-judge calibration against human-annotated samples and recalibration whenever task content, network topology, or base models change.
extraction.limitations: A practitioner guidance report rather than an empirical study: it contributes no experiments, datasets, measured effect sizes, or validated instruments, and the authors position the techniques as adaptable tools rather than a prescriptive framework. Scope is restricted to governed environments where a single organisation controls the configuration and deployment of all agents, so open, cross-organisational, or adversarial multi-agent ecosystems are excluded. The authors acknowledge fundamental limits in the scientific understanding of LLM behaviour, so practitioners can only progressively increase validity rather than establish it. Translation from risk analysis to risk evaluation and treatment is left highly contextual and organisation-specific. Coverage of catastrophic risk, security, privacy, and human-AI interaction is discussed only briefly.
